stem: A clinic has Patients(pid) rows 1, 2 and 3. Visits(pid,fee) contains (1,100), (1,200), (2,NULL). With no filters, an analyst LEFT JOINs Patients to Visits on pid. What are COUNT(*), COUNT(Visits.fee) and SUM(Visits.fee) over the joined rows?
solution: Patient 1 produces two joined rows, patient 2 one, and unmatched patient 3 one. COUNT(*) is 4. Two fee values are observed, and their sum is 300. NULL is not a measured zero.

option_explanations.A: The repeated patient 1 produces an extra row; COUNT(fee) excludes NULL.
option_explanations.B: Correct: 4 joined rows, 2 observed fees, sum 300.
option_explanations.C: COUNT(fee) counts only non-NULL fee values.
option_explanations.D: The query is a sum, not an average, and the join returns 4 rows.

source_references.locator: Independently authored scenario; concept support only

learning_objective: Trace a LEFT JOIN and distinguish row count from non-NULL count
difficulty_rationale: Combine the stated assumptions with the business interpretation.

stem: A booking table has room_id INT, day DATE, optional note TEXT, and PRIMARY KEY(room_id,day). It has no other constraints and contains (7,'2026-10-22'). Each following INSERT runs independently under autocommit. Which statements are correct? Select ALL.

choices.text: (7,'2026-10-23') is allowed with note omitted.
(8,'2026-10-22') is allowed with note omitted.
Another (7,'2026-10-22') is allowed if its note differs.
(NULL,'2026-10-24') is allowed if its note is supplied.

solution: The full pair must be unique, and both key components must be non-NULL. Neither component alone must be unique. The optional note does not change the key.

option_explanations.A: Correct: a new day creates a new pair; optional note may be NULL.
option_explanations.B: Correct: a different room creates a new pair.
option_explanations.C: The key pair repeats, regardless of note.
option_explanations.D: A primary-key component cannot be NULL.

source_references.locator: Independently authored scenario; concept support only

difficulty_rationale: Combine the stated assumptions with the business interpretation.

stem: A subscription team measures monthly support minutes for the same 30 customers before and after a redesigned help page. A suitable paired test gives a mean reduction of 4 minutes and a 95% interval from 1 to 7 minutes. Customers were not randomly assigned to a control group. Which recommendation is most defensible?

choices.text: Roll out immediately: the interval proves every customer saves time.
Use an independent-samples test because there are two measurements.
Treat the reduction as evidence worth investigating, check cost and seasonality, and use a controlled pilot before a causal claim.
Conclude there is no effect because some other explanations remain.

solution: The paired observations support a mean-change analysis. The interval excludes zero under its assumptions, but it is not an interval for every customer and does not remove time-related confounding.

option_explanations.A: The interval estimates mean change, not each customer’s change.
option_explanations.B: The same customers are measured twice, so the observations are paired.
option_explanations.C: Correct: distinguish statistical evidence, causality and business benefit.
option_explanations.D: Possible confounding does not erase the observed mean-change evidence.

source_references.locator: Independently authored scenario; concept support only

learning_objective: Separate paired statistical evidence from a causal rollout decision
difficulty_rationale: Combine the stated assumptions with the business interpretation.

stem: An illustrative monthly sales model is Y = 10 + 2A + 3H + A×H, in ₹ lakh. A is advertising spend in ₹ lakh and H=1 for a city store, 0 for a town store. Treat the equation as a prediction model, not a causal estimate. Which statements are correct? Select ALL.

choices.text: The advertising slope is 2 for town stores and 3 for city stores.
At A=4, the predicted city-town sales gap is 7 lakh.
The city-town gap is always 3 lakh, regardless of advertising.
The coefficient 2 proves a causal return of two rupees for every advertising rupee.

solution: Town sales are 10+2A; city sales are 13+3A. Their gap is 3+A, hence 7 at A=4. The equation alone does not identify a causal effect.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the interaction adds 1 to the slope when H=1.
option_explanations.C: The interaction makes the gap depend on A.
option_explanations.D: A fitted conditional association is not automatically causal.

source_references.locator: Independently authored scenario; concept support only

learning_objective: Compute group-specific slopes and a conditional format difference

stem: A meal-delivery app reduces cancellations from 12% to 8% after offering a ₹40 voucher on every completed order. The finance team finds contribution per eligible visitor fell. Management asks whether the voucher should become permanent. What is the best next analysis?

choices.text: Compare incremental contribution per eligible visitor in a controlled pilot, including voucher cost and retention.
Keep the voucher because cancellation is the only relevant metric.
Stop all analysis because a lower cancellation rate proves the voucher failed.
Compare only revenue among customers who completed an order.

solution: The decision concerns net business value, not one favourable rate. A comparable controlled pilot with voucher costs and retention can estimate incremental contribution and expose tradeoffs.

option_explanations.A: Correct: it addresses the decision and includes the cost of the intervention.
option_explanations.B: A single operational metric does not settle profitability.
option_explanations.C: A lower cancellation rate may be useful even if the current subsidy is too costly.
option_explanations.D: Conditioning only on completed orders ignores changes in conversion and cost.

learning_objective: Select a decision-relevant evaluation metric with guardrails
difficulty_rationale: Combine the stated assumptions with the business interpretation.

stem: A distributor has two product groups. Group A records revenue ₹80,000 and profit ₹8,000. Group B records revenue ₹20,000 and profit ₹6,000. Management wants the overall profit margin. Which statements are correct? Select ALL.

choices.text: The overall margin is 14%, using total profit divided by total revenue.
The unweighted mean of group margins is 20% and equals the overall margin.
Group B has the higher margin but the lower absolute profit.
A chart of sales alone establishes that Group A is more profitable in percentage terms.

solution: Total profit is 14,000 and total revenue 100,000, giving 14%. Group margins are 10% and 30%; their unweighted mean of 20% answers a different question.

option_explanations.B: The group revenue weights differ, so 20% is not the overall margin.
option_explanations.D: Sales without profit cannot establish percentage profitability.

source_references.locator: Independently authored scenario; concept support only

learning_objective: Distinguish weighted overall margin from a simple mean of group ratios
difficulty_rationale: Combine the stated assumptions with the business interpretation.
